summary: Defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for managing SCSI entities, independent of the underlying interconnect. Network management tools can use it to inspect storage devices and their initiators and targets. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A set of labelled dials for checking on computer storage gear from afar without needing to go and look at the box.

questions: how to monitor scsi devices with snmp
what is a scsi initiator and target
subtitle: An SNMP MIB module for configuring and monitoring SCSI initiators, targets and ports, whatever interconnect they use.

tldr.problem: Storage networks have SCSI initiator devices, target devices, ports and logical units that administrators need to inspect and control remotely, across different transports such as iSCSI and Fibre Channel.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4455 defines the SCSI-MIB module for SNMP. It models the SCSI protocol layer common to all transports and command sets, in fourteen conformance groups of tables for devices, ports, discovery, LUN mapping and statistics.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard. Transport-specific details are left to other MIB modules, which link to it through a SCSI port table, and the RFC recommends SNMPv3 because many objects are sensitive.

facts.label: Notification limit
facts.value: No more than 3 in any 10-second period

today: RFC 4455 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2006, and the metadata for this entry lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its text refers to an iSCSI MIB that was still a work in progress when it was published.

sections.title: What the SCSI MIB Is For
sections.content:
This memo defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for network management. It describes managed objects to configure and monitor SCSI entities: SCSI target devices, SCSI initiator devices and SCSI ports. They are accessed with SNMP, and the module is written in SMIv2.

SCSI is a client-server protocol. Application clients in an initiator device (the client) send service requests to logical units in a target device (the server). The MIB follows the ANSI T10 documents SCSI Architecture Model-2 (SAM-2) and SCSI Primary Commands-2 (SPC-2), and SAM-2 is the main source for its terminology.

The RFC gives a short history. SCSI began as an 8-bit multi-drop bus that interconnected a total of eight peripherals and computer systems. Later work separated command sets from the physical interface, which led to the architecture model, and to Fibre Channel and iSCSI as ways to carry SCSI over other networks.
sections.eli5: Storage boxes talk to computers in a special language called SCSI. This document makes a standard way for a manager to ask those boxes how they are doing.

sections.title: SCSI Terminology and Instances
sections.content:
The RFC explains the SAM-2 terms it uses. A SCSI device has one or more SCSI ports connected to a service delivery subsystem. A SCSI port is either an initiator port or a target port. An initiator device holds application clients and initiator ports; a target device holds logical units and target ports. A logical unit implements a device model and processes SCSI commands, and a Logical Unit Number (LUN) is a 64-bit identifier for it.

A SCSI instance is a distinct SCSI entity within a managed system. Most implementations have just one, but the MIB allows several virtual instances, so a large system can be partitioned into distinct virtual systems, or several vendors' implementations can share one SNMP agent.

Many objects are labelled local or remote. Local entities are those the agent reports on; remote entities are those they communicate with over SCSI. The MIB does not represent SCSI domains, because they usually cannot be determined from within a system.
sections.eli5: A computer that asks for data is the customer, and the storage box that has the data is the shop. Each shop has numbered shelves called logical units, and the MIB keeps track of which customers use which shelves.

sections.title: Where the MIB Sits and How It Is Deployed
sections.content:
The SCSI MIB represents only the SCSI protocol layer shared by all command sets and transports. It does not represent the command sets or transports themselves. Those belong in other MIB modules, such as an iSCSI MIB or a Fibre Channel MIB. A transport MIB is tied to the SCSI MIB through the SCSI port table, which has an object pointing to the matching row in the transport MIB, if there is one. The module also extends the Host Resources MIB for SCSI-specific entities.

The module is meant to be implemented in every SCSI entity in a managed system, whether initiator, target or both. The RFC shows three scenarios: one initiator and one target, each with its own SNMP agent; several hosts and a single target; and an in-band virtualization device that includes both target and initiator functionality, so its MIB holds both sets of objects. The SCSI MIB does not distinguish between physical and virtual SCSI entities.

Configuration of bridging and virtualization devices is outside its scope and should be provided through other MIB modules. Management of SCSI commands is also out of scope.
sections.eli5: This MIB covers the part of the conversation that is the same for every kind of cable. Anything special to one kind of cable gets its own separate set of dials.

sections.title: The Fourteen Conformance Groups
sections.content:
The module is organized into fourteen conformance groups. The core ones are:

  • scsiDeviceGroup: instance, device, port and transport objects. It is mandatory for every SCSI managed system.
  • scsiInitiatorDeviceGroup: information on local initiator devices and ports, plus the attached target devices they monitor. Any system acting as an initiator or target/initiator MUST support it.
  • scsiTargetDeviceGroup: local target devices and ports, attached initiator ports, logical units and their identifiers. Systems acting as a target or target/initiator must support it.
  • scsiDiscoveryGroup: remote target devices, ports and logical units discovered by or configured on an initiator.
  • scsiLunMapGroup: mapping from target devices, logical units and LUNs to authorized remote initiators.

The other nine groups hold statistics for targets, LUN maps, initiators, discovery and devices. Four of them are "high speed" variants for systems that generate countable information quickly. Systems able to gather the statistics should implement the matching groups.

Alias objects for instances and devices use the SnmpAdminString textual convention, so administrators can give them readable names.
sections.eli5: The dials are sorted into fourteen labelled boxes. Every storage system must have the basic box, and the other boxes are for the things it actually does.

sections.title: How the Tables Work Together
sections.content:
The RFC lists the features an initiator side needs and the tables that provide them. The initiator port table lists the initiator ports to manage. The discovery target table lists the target ports or devices an initiator port may attach to, created manually or by automatic discovery such as SLP or iSNS. This keeps an initiator away from targets that should be invisible or inaccessible to it. Related tables give the logical units and LUN identifiers of those targets, and the attached target port table shows what each initiator port is currently talking to.

On the target side, the target port table lists the target ports. The authorized initiator table works like the access lists common in IP routers and switches: it says which initiators may attach to a target port. Each entry has a pointer, scsiAuthIntrLunMapIndex, into the LUN map table, so each initiator can be shown its own list of LUNs or the default list. The attached initiator port table shows who is connected now.

The MIB permits, but does not require, SNMP writes to the discovery and authorization tables, and warns of significant security considerations if they are allowed.
sections.eli5: There is a guest list saying which computers may visit each storage box, and a menu for each guest saying which shelves they may see. Another list shows who is visiting right now.

sections.title: Counters and Notifications
sections.content:
Fast systems can make a 32-bit counter wrap in less than an hour, so the module defines such counters as both Counter32 and Counter64. Older SNMPv1 implementations cannot support Counter64, which is why both exist. Counters of data are measured in megabytes so no 64-bit counter is needed for them. Counters of commands could wrap within an hour at 5 GBit/second with 512-byte operations, so each has both forms, and the 64-bit one is mandatory for systems of 4 Gbit/second or higher.

Separate SNMP notifications can be enabled or disabled for changes in SCSI device status. To avoid floods, an agent should not send more than three SCSI notifications in any 10-second period. The RFC explains that this allows a short burst without swamping the network or the receiving host.
sections.eli5: A counter is like a car odometer that can run out of digits and start over. Very busy systems get a bigger odometer, and the alarm may only ring a few times in a short span so nobody gets deafened.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some objects are read-write or read-create, and setting them without protection can hurt network operation. The RFC names the aliases, the notification switch and storage type, scsiIntrDevTgtAccessMode, and the discovery target, authorized initiator and LUN map tables. Changing the last four can remove administrator-set access controls, give an initiator logical units that were meant to be hidden, or cause denial of service by blocking authorized access.

Readable objects can be sensitive too. All seventeen tables contain information that may be sensitive to read, such as software versions, topology, LUN exposure and mapping, and statistics usable for traffic analysis.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC RECOMMENDS the SNMPv3 security features, including its cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, and says deploying versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators must configure access so that only legitimate principals can GET or SET the objects.
sections.eli5: These dials can reveal which storage is where and who may use it, and some dials can even change who is allowed in. So only the right people should be able to see or turn them, and the secure version of SNMP should be used.

sections.title: Worked Example: A Disk on a Parallel SCSI Bus
sections.content:
The RFC includes a non-normative example showing how the tables could be filled in for a parallel SCSI bus. The initiator device is a Host Bus Adaptor (HBA) and the target device is a physical disk with one logical unit at LUN 0, the default LUN. Parallel SCSI has port identifiers but no port names, and the transport pointer is set to 0 because no transport MIB exists for SPI-4.

The example then walks through the table rows, such as the instance table with alias pSCSI-1 and the device table with the aliases pSCSI-HBA and pSCSI-Disk1. The RFC says it is based on assumptions rather than on actual implementations.
sections.eli5: The example fills in the forms for a tiny setup, one computer card and one disk, so you can see what the filled-in dials look like.
